answer.label: Not Machiavelli — actually Newt Gingrich
answer.authorDates: b. 17 June 1943 · U.S. Representative from Georgia; House Minority Whip in 1991
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line in its Misattributed section for Machiavelli and identifies it as Newt Gingrich’s, first appearing in a Los Angeles Times article in 1991. Machiavelli, who wrote in Italian and died in 1527, did not write it — and the sentiment runs against The Prince, which treats overturning an existing order as the most dangerous thing a ruler can attempt.

trail: Wikiquote’s Machiavelli page ↗ lists “I am not interested in preserving the status quo; I want to overthrow it” in its Misattributed section, describing it as a quote by Newt Gingrich, first appearing in an article in the Los Angeles Times in 1991.

Don MacDonald’s 2011 post ↗ identifies that article as the origin “as near as I can tell,” dates it 25 August 1991, quotes the sentence, and notes that the phrasing including the semicolon matches the version circulating under Machiavelli’s name.

Ian Chadwick’s Machiavellian Misquotes ↗, an appendix to his book on Machiavelli, independently states that Machiavelli did not write it and that it comes from a 1991 LA Times interview with Gingrich.
Checking the other direction: the phrase “status quo” appears nowhere in the full text of The Prince ↗ in W. K. Marriott’s translation, published in 1908 by J. M. Dent & Sons and E. P. Dutton ↗.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed from the 25 August 1991 Los Angeles Times article by Don MacDonald ↗; “he” is Newt Gingrich. The original article page is no longer live on the LA Times site, so this transcription and Wikiquote’s citation ↗ are the documentation we can show.
source.rightsHolder: Los Angeles Times (article text); Newt Gingrich (spoken remarks)
source.rightsNote: The only documented appearance of this sentence is a Los Angeles Times article of 25 August 1991, which is well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff and remains in copyright to the newspaper. Machiavelli’s own works and W. K. Marriott’s 1908 translation of The Prince are public domain — but this line is in neither of them, so no public-domain status attaches to it.

author.name: Newt Gingrich
author.heading: Who actually said it
author.metaLine: b. 1943 · U.S. Representative from Georgia 1979–1999 · House Minority Whip in 1991 · Speaker of the House 1995–1999
author.bio: Newton Leroy Gingrich, born in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania on 17 June 1943, represented Georgia in the U.S. House from 1979 to 1999. He became House Minority Whip in March 1989 — the post he held when the Los Angeles Times quoted him in 1991 — and served as Speaker of the House from January 1995 to January 1999. The line is characteristic of the insurgent, anti-institutional posture that defined his rise, which is exactly why it travels so well once someone swaps in a more glamorous name.

misattribution.heading: How a 1991 newspaper line became a Renaissance aphorism
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case: the quote has a documented modern speaker, and the transfer to Machiavelli left fingerprints — including an unchanged semicolon.

items.why: Goodreads, BrainyQuote and QuoteFancy all carry the line under Machiavelli’s name with no work, chapter, translator or date attached. Goodreads’ own page ↗ notes that its quotes are added by the community and are not verified.

Wikiquote ↗ records the line as Gingrich’s, first appearing in a Los Angeles Times article in 1991. Don MacDonald ↗ located that article, dated 25 August 1991, and pointed out that the punctuation of the internet version — semicolon included — matches the newspaper sentence exactly.

The Prince argues the opposite emphasis. Chapter VI warns that “there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things” (Marriott translation ↗) — a warning about the cost of upheaval, not an appetite for it.
Machiavelli wrote in Italian, and the Latin tag “status quo” appears nowhere in W. K. Marriott’s standard English text of The Prince ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line belongs to a 20th-century American politician, not a 16th-century Florentine official: Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed ↗ and credits Newt Gingrich, first printed in the Los Angeles Times in 1991.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: The quote works as a Machiavelli quote because of what we think Machiavelli was: a cold-eyed disruptor who taught princes to break things. The actual Machiavelli was a career civil servant — secretary of the second chancery of Florence from 1498 to 1512 — who spent his exile writing manuals on how rulers take power and keep it, and on how ruinous upheaval usually is. The Prince, drafted around 1513 and not published until 1532, five years after his death, opens its most famous warning by saying there is nothing more difficult or perilous than taking the lead in introducing a new order of things. That is a caution, not a battle cry.

The man who actually said it was in the business of overthrowing something specific. In 1991 Newt Gingrich was House Minority Whip, four years out from the speakership he would take in January 1995. Strip his name off and the sentence loses its target and becomes a general-purpose slogan — which is precisely the condition in which a line drifts onto a Renaissance philosopher.
detailsBody: Even the fake has variants. Wikiquote’s misattributed entry reads “I am not interested in preserving the status quo…”, while the wording transcribed from the 1991 article — and the form Goodreads and QuoteFancy carry — is the contracted “I’m not…”. The semicolon survives every version, which is part of what let researchers match the internet meme back to the newspaper sentence.

There is also a vocabulary problem. “Status quo” is a Latin tag that entered English political usage centuries after Machiavelli, who wrote in Italian; it appears nowhere in W. K. Marriott’s standard 1908 English translation of The Prince.
context.pull: Machiavelli’s warning about a “new order of things” is about how dangerous change is. The fake quote makes him its cheerleader.
